hints.hint: First write, for each speaker, exactly what they see and what stays unknown to them. If the problem never says which quantity the public number is, that role is unknown to them too, so no speaker may just subtract or divide to pin the partner. For each possible private value v, list the partners allowed under every reading, dropping those that break the domain rules (natural number, exact division). One survivor means "I know"; two or more means "I don't know". Turn each announcement into the set of v it permits, then apply later announcements only to those survivors. If every reading looks contradictory, you gave a speaker knowledge they lack: fix the unknown list rather than guessing a plausible value to fill the answer.

For (z-a)^n = c(z-b)^n (b may be 0), do not enumerate the n roots. Take moduli: every root obeys |z-a| = k|z-b|, k = |c|^(1/n). If k = 1 the locus is the perpendicular bisector of a and b: a line, not a circle. Otherwise it is an Apollonius circle, and the fastest data comes from dropping the bars along line ab: solve z-a = k(z-b) and z-a = -k(z-b). Those two points are opposite ends of a diameter, so center = their midpoint, radius = half their distance. Cross-check once with z = x+iy: square, collect x^2+y^2, divide by its coefficient, complete the square. The center is off the origin and not on the circle itself, so |z| varies; that is expected. Report exactly the quantity asked.

Union = areas summed minus overlap, so minimize overlap. Put the shared point at the origin and settle membership by signed half-plane tests. A corner placed at an interior point of shape S covers a wedge there, so the overlap is positive and strictly less than S: reject any claim that they touch in one point or that one lies wholly inside the other. Prove invariance rather than sampling angles. If that point is a k-fold rotational-symmetry center of S and the wedge angle is exactly 2*pi/k with both edges exiting S, rotation by 2*pi/k maps S to itself and sends the wedge to the next one, so the k wedge positions cut S into k equal pieces. Overlap is then area(S)/k at every rotation, so minimum equals maximum: compute that one area, report the union, stop. Build a piecewise area function and test its breakpoints only if the wedge angle differs from 2*pi/k.

When each term of the required pattern may come from any of N given functions, never compare adjacent terms: neighbours can use different functions, so that route yields no bound. Write the pattern's value at index n as an explicit T(n), then partition indices by which function produced them. On one function P's group, P - T vanishes and is not identically zero, since subtracting the low-degree T cannot cancel P's leading term; so that group holds at most deg P indices. Hence Bound = N x deg P. Trust that product even if it looks too large for a contest; do not shrink or re-derive it. Instead verify by construction: give each function its own block of consecutive indices and interpolate T's values there - matching that many points leaves coefficients free, so a legal function exists. Bound plus construction is the whole proof; then answer.

Fit unknown parameters first: rewrite each given point in exponential form (log_c u = y means u = c^y) and solve the resulting system. For the unknown vertices, use the vector condition to write one as a translation of a variable point, then subtract the two log equations so only a ratio of arguments survives: a y-difference d becomes argument factor c^d. With base under 1 this inverts the naive direction, so test that ratio relation on the known points before solving. A negative discriminant, or roots outside the domain, means an orientation, sign, or branch choice is wrong: flip it and redo once instead of re-verifying the same arithmetic. Get the area as the absolute cross product of adjacent edge vectors.

Describe a configuration by the ordered contents of the truck, gate, and shed rather than by informal move sequences. Legal moves form a small state graph; at each state, attach the actual transition probability, noting that it changes when only one move is available. Propagate probabilities by dynamic programming while retaining enough label order to test the requested final event. Check that probabilities, rather than merely path counts, sum to one.

Interpret the unknown coefficients as weights of a linear functional evaluated at distinct nodes. The vanishing moment conditions say that this functional annihilates a long range of monomials, while the next moment fixes its scale. Apply Lagrange interpolation after any useful index shift: the leading coefficient gives a product-of-node-differences formula for each weight. Simplify only the requested endpoint weight and verify the highest prescribed moment.

Let N be the unstated count of identical units, and recover it from integrality rather than from the story: if every per-unit share must be a whole number, N divides each listed total, so the admissible N are their common divisors and the intended one is the maximum feasible count, namely their gcd. Wording about identical equal groups only requires N to be a multiple of the group count; verify it and do not treat it as fixing N. Decide once whether each listed figure is a grand total or a per-unit amount, then stop revisiting it. Finally add all component amounts, divide by N, and apply any stated markup or discount as a single multiplicative factor; scaling and dividing commute, so either order is fine. Check that every per-unit value is a whole number and that the units match what was asked.

If p(q(x))=q(p(x)) with p,q the same degree n, do not grind the degree-n^2 coefficient system - that is where attempts stall and run out of room. Instead look for a common fixed point r and try the jointly centered form p(x)=r+A(x-r)^n, q(x)=r+B(x-r)^n. Composing forces AB^n=BA^n; factor that once as AB(A^(n-1)-B^(n-1))=0 and carry both branches, since B=A collapses to p=q. Let the given data, not a guessed sign, kill a branch. On the sign-flipped branch the given values combine symmetrically: their sum cancels the (x-r)^n terms and pins r, their difference pins A. Verify p(r)=q(r)=r and check the identity at one spare point. Then evaluate only the requested inputs in centered form, never expanding.

For "how many repeats restore the original" problems, simulate; don't theorize. Write the state as distinct labels and do each listed sub-step by rewriting the whole state: swapping two adjacent blocks concatenates them in the other order and leaves the rest fixed. Fix ONE convention (slot i now holds label X) and never mix in its inverse (label at i goes to slot j); that mix-up makes correct work look self-contradictory. After each sub-step check every label appears once. Never assume overlapping sub-steps compose to an involution or to disjoint swaps. Then repeat the full operation, counting until the state first returns to the original; cross-check against the lcm of the disjoint cycle lengths. Do the two smallest sizes exactly, propose a closed form, test it on one larger size, and if a size disagrees redo that simulation instead of patching the formula piecewise.
